name: Goal Zero Lighthouse 600 Lantern
summary: The lantern to light your main room through a multi-day outage, with a crank and USB output as useful extras.
verdict: The Lighthouse 600 is the lantern we would put at the center of a household outage kit. Goal Zero rates it at up to 600 lumens, which is far more than a living room needs, and that headroom is the point: run it at a third of maximum and it lights the room comfortably while the built-in battery lasts for nights rather than hours. The dimmer is a dial rather than a few fixed steps, and you can choose to light both sides of the lantern or just one, which halves the drain when the lantern sits against a wall. It recharges over USB from anything you have, including a car, a power bank or a solar panel, and a fold-out hand crank gives you emergency light if every battery in the house is flat. A USB output lets it top up a phone in a pinch. The folding legs and hanging handle make it easy to place where light spreads best.

name: BioLite AlpenGlow 500 Lantern
summary: The most pleasant lantern to spend an evening with; choose it over the Goal Zero if light quality matters more than a crank.
verdict: Most emergency lanterns are designed for brightness first and comfort second. The AlpenGlow 500 flips that. BioLite rates it at up to 500 lumens, but its real strength is the quality of light at lower settings: a warm white mode and a candle-flicker mode that give a room the feel of a lamp rather than an interrogation. The frosted body diffuses light evenly, so a moderate setting lights a living room without glare, which is exactly where runtime is best. It recharges over USB and can share its battery with a phone through a USB output, though as with any lantern that comes at the cost of light later on. There is no crank and no solar panel, so plan to recharge it from a power bank or power station in a long outage. The color-cycling modes are fun for kids but not a reason to buy it. Buy it because it makes a dark house feel normal.
skipIf: No hand crank or built-in solar

name: Coleman 400 Lumen LED Lantern
summary: The closet backup that works after years in storage, provided you keep the D cells beside it rather than inside it.
verdict: Coleman has been making camp lanterns for generations, and its 400 lumen LED lantern is the kind of light that suits a disposable-battery backup role perfectly. It runs on D-cell batteries, which hold several times the energy of AAs, so a fresh set gives long runtime at a moderate setting, and when they run low you simply swap in new ones rather than waiting for the power to come back. The 400 lumen maximum, per Coleman, is plenty for a room, and the lantern is built for outdoor use, so it shrugs off rough handling. Its weaknesses are the weaknesses of every battery lantern: it is heavy, it has no USB port, and alkaline D cells left inside for years can leak and ruin the contacts. Store the batteries in their packaging next to the lantern and check them at the same time you check the smoke alarms. It is not the nicest light in this guide, but it is one of the most dependable.

Batteries can be swapped in seconds, no grid required
Simple, rugged design from a long-established brand

name: LuminAID PackLite Max 2-in-1 Solar Lantern
summary: The best light for a week-long grid-down outage or a car kit, as long as you can put it in direct sun.
verdict: LuminAID started out making inflatable solar lights for disaster relief, and the PackLite Max 2-in-1 is the grown-up version of that idea. It packs flat to roughly the thickness of a paperback, inflates into a soft lantern that diffuses light well, and recharges itself from a solar panel on top. LuminAID rates it at up to 150 lumens, which is enough for a bedroom or a tent, and the 2-in-1 model can also recharge over USB and add a small charge to a phone. That combination makes it the light most likely to still be working at the end of a long outage when every other battery is spent. Be realistic about solar: it needs a full day of direct sun to recharge well, and a cloudy window sill will not do it. It also floats and is designed to be waterproof, which matters after a flood. As a main room light it is too dim; as a backup that never needs batteries, it is excellent.

name: Goal Zero Lighthouse Micro Flash Lantern
summary: An inexpensive personal light: give one to every member of the household and keep the big lantern for the main room.
verdict: The Lighthouse Micro Flash is a small cylinder about the size of a roll of coins that works as both a lantern and a flashlight. Goal Zero rates it at up to 150 lumens, which is plenty for a bedroom, a bathroom or a walk to the garage, and its built-in battery recharges over USB from a wall adapter, a car or a power bank. The main reason to buy it is that it is cheap enough to buy several, which solves the most common outage problem: one good light and several people who need it. Hang one from a bedroom door handle with its loop and nobody has to fumble for a phone at three in the morning. There is no phone-charging output and the battery is not replaceable, so it is a personal light rather than a backbone of the kit. Pair it with a larger lantern for shared spaces and keep it on the same twice-a-year recharge schedule as everything else.
skipIf: Too small to light a large room

name: Black Diamond Moji Lantern
summary: A cheap, cheerful personal lantern for children, bathrooms and hallways rather than the main room.
verdict: The Moji is a palm-sized lantern with a frosted globe that turns a small amount of light into a soft, even glow, which is exactly what a child's bedroom or a bathroom needs in an outage. Black Diamond sells it in several versions, including ones that run on AAA batteries and rechargeable versions, and output varies between them, so read the listing to see which you are getting. It is not bright enough to light a kitchen for cooking or a basement for checking a sump pump, and it does not try to be. What it does well is hang anywhere from its built-in hook, survive being dropped by a seven-year-old, and give everyone in the household their own light without spending much. If you choose the AAA version, standardize on the same cells as your other small lights and store spares in the kit. For hallways and bathrooms, its gentle light is easier on sleepy eyes than a bright lantern.

name: Black Diamond Spot 400 Headlamp
summary: Every adult in the house should have a headlamp, and the Spot 400 is a proven, well-built default.
verdict: A headlamp is the light you will wish you had the first time you try to carry a bucket, reset a breaker or check the basement in an outage while holding a phone in your mouth. The Black Diamond Spot 400 is one of the most popular hiking headlamps for good reasons: Black Diamond rates it at up to 400 lumens, it runs on common AAA batteries, and it is built to be waterproof, so it survives a trip outside to check a storm-damaged fence. A red light mode lets you move around at night without waking anyone or wrecking your night vision, and a dimmable output lets you trade brightness for runtime. Black Diamond also sells a rechargeable Spot 400-R version if you prefer USB charging. It is not a room light; its beam is designed to go where you look. That is precisely why it belongs in the kit alongside a lantern rather than instead of one.
skipIf: Focused beam does not light a whole room
